title: Activations and derivatives
description: Substitute into all four lecture activation formulas, understand slopes, and practise the chain rule.
source_short: Lecture 3 / PDF p.156; Assignment 1 / PDF p.2 / zero convention stated
source: Lecture 3 - Learning Neural Network.pdf, page 156; Assignment 1.pdf, page 2. Original numerical inputs.

pages.title: An activation and its slope are different
pages.subtitle: Lecture 3, PDF page 156 lists the four functions and their derivatives.
blocks: z is the weighted input before activation. We write a for the activation; the notes often write y. Here a is not a known target label.
The derivative is the local slope: how much the activation changes for a tiny increase in z.
Our main input is z = ln(3). Natural logarithm ln(3) means the number whose exponential is 3. This choice makes hand arithmetic simple.

pages.title: Sigmoid: calculate the activation first
pages.subtitle: The output is between zero and one; its derivative is a different number.
blocks: A small increase of 0.01 in input changes this activation by about 0.001875. This is a local approximation, not an exact finite difference.

pages.title: Tanh: use the two exponential values
pages.subtitle: The assignment gives this exponential form; the lecture gives the derivative.
blocks: Square the activation before subtracting it from 1. The formula is not (1 - a) squared. Unlike sigmoid, tanh may output negative values.

pages.title: ReLU: choose the correct branch
pages.subtitle: ReLU means rectified linear unit: keep positive input, otherwise output zero.
blocks: At a positive input, increasing z by 0.01 increases the activation by exactly 0.01 as long as both inputs remain positive.
Zero is a special point where the classical derivative does not exist. We will compare the source conventions explicitly.

pages.title: Softplus: a smooth positive activation
pages.subtitle: Use the natural logarithm, not a base-10 calculator logarithm.
blocks: Softplus and sigmoid have different outputs. Softplus has sigmoid as its derivative; do not replace its activation by sigmoid.

pages.title: Negative input: sigmoid and tanh
pages.subtitle: Now z = -ln(3), so exp(z) = 1/3 and exp(-z) = 3.
blocks: The activation of tanh is negative, but its slope here is positive. A negative activation does not imply a negative derivative.

pages.title: Negative input: ReLU and softplus
pages.subtitle: The two functions behave differently on the negative side.
blocks: ReLU is flat for strictly negative input. Softplus is smooth and still has a small positive output and slope.

pages.title: At zero: three smooth functions
pages.subtitle: Substitute exp(0) = 1 before calculating the derivatives.
blocks: Zero activation and zero derivative are different claims. Tanh has activation 0 at the origin but slope 1.

pages.title: ReLU at zero: reconcile the two sources
pages.subtitle: The left and right slopes disagree, so there is no classical derivative.
blocks: Lecture 3, PDF page 156 assigns slope 1 when z >= 0. Assignment 1, PDF page 2 assigns slope 1 only when z > 0, otherwise 0.
These are chosen backpropagation conventions at the kink, not classical derivatives. For assignment-aligned work, use 0 at zero and state that convention.

pages.title: Compare the activation curves
pages.subtitle: Same input z, different outputs and local slopes.
blocks: Sigmoid and tanh flatten near their upper and lower limits. ReLU has a corner at zero. Softplus smoothly bends from a near-flat negative side to a near-linear positive side.

pages.title: Saturation means a small local slope
pages.subtitle: At z = 4 the smooth bounded activations change slowly; their slopes are not zero.
blocks: At zero the same small input change gives about 0.0025 for sigmoid and 0.01 for tanh. Repeated small slope factors can shrink gradients in a deep network.

pages.title: Use the local slope in the chain rule
pages.subtitle: Suppose the incoming loss derivative is dL/da = 2 at z = ln(3).
blocks: The incoming derivative depends on the rest of the network and loss. Here it is a supplied value, used to isolate the role of the activation derivative.

pages.title: Your turn: an input with simple exponentials
pages.subtitle: Use z = ln(2), so exp(z) = 2 and exp(-z) = 1/2.
blocks: For sigmoid, tanh, ReLU and softplus, calculate both the activation and its local derivative. Show the substitutions before simplifying.
Then suppose dL/da = -3. Calculate dL/dz for each activation using the chain rule.
Finally, state the derivative convention you would use for ReLU at zero in Assignment 1, and why it is a convention.

pages.title: Practice answer: sigmoid and tanh
pages.subtitle: Keep exact fractions until the final result.

pages.title: Practice answer: ReLU and softplus
pages.subtitle: The sign of the loss derivative comes from the incoming value -3.
blocks: Assignment 1 uses ReLU slope 0 at zero. Its left and right slopes are 0 and 1, so the usual derivative does not exist there.
Checklist: do not confuse activation with slope, tanh derivative with (1-a)^2, or softplus output with sigmoid output.
